newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: EU struggles to respond to Albania crisis.
newsitem.headline: EU struggles to respond to Albania crisis.

text.p: The European Union struggled on Saturday to find an answer to Albania's request for military intervention.

Foreign ministers of the 15-member bloc, still stinging from criticism of their indecision over the last Balkan conflict, in former Yugoslavia, discussed Albania's slide into anarchy for five hours at an informal meeting in the central Dutch town of Apeldoorn.
They were set to send a mission to Albania and edged towards agreement on the concept of supplying police advisers.
But talk of a 4,000-strong peacekeeping force met vehement opposition from Germany, Britain and Sweden.
"The EU is committed to helping Albania help itself," the Dutch EU presidency said in a draft communique released during the two-day meeting.
Ministers said they were considering sending a small police force to advise the Albanian authorities.
Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said the small force would be sent if the EU received a United Nations mandate. He stressed this was not the same as military intervention.
But his Danish and German colleagues insisted there was no final agreement even on this, saying ministers would return to the issue on Sunday.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette also played down talk that this token force would be a peacekeeping operation.
"It's out of the question that this would be an international force which would restore law and order in the towns and villages of Albania," he told reporters.
Supported by Germany, Britain firmly opposed sending any sizeable force, the option favoured by OSCE mediator Franz Vranitzky who met Albanian authorities on an Italian ship on Friday.

"There is no way any military commander in any serious western country would envisage sending two to three thousand troops into Albania to try and restore law and order under the current circumstances," one British diplomat said.

Carl Bildt, the international community's Bosnia representative, added to the pressure for EU action by saying that failure to act would make current discussion on EU joint foreign and security policy look "pathetic".
The session ended abruptly when a report arrived that Albania's President Sali Berisha had resigned -- a report later denied from Tirana.
Ministers immediately shelved plans to work late into the evening and departed for dinner.
They were due to return on Sunday to put the finishing touches to their Albanian response before moving on to discussing plans to admit former communist states and prickly relations with Turkey.
